title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 9
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Full practice tests
summary: A full, timed Reading and Writing section in Digital SAT format: two 32-minute modules of 27 questions each, with an explanation for every answer choice and your score by skill.

blocks.text: This is a complete Reading and Writing section in the format of the Digital SAT: **two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each (54 questions, 64 minutes)**. Every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four choices. Inside each module the questions come in the usual order: Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, and Expression of Ideas last. All passages and questions were written for this course.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone and about 70 minutes free. Do the whole test in one sitting.
The timer starts when you begin a module. Aim for about 1 minute 11 seconds per question, and do not spend more than 2 minutes on any single question.

Inside a module you can move back and forth between questions. When the 32 minutes end, the module closes. In the real test, you cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts, so treat this test the same way.
There is no penalty for wrong answers. Never leave a question blank: if time is short, eliminate what you can and guess.
At the end you will see your number correct, your result for each module and each skill, and an explanation for every question.

blocks.title: About your result
blocks.text: The score shown at the end is a practice percentage (the number of questions you answered correctly). It is not an official SAT score. Official Reading and Writing scores are reported on a scale of 200–800, and this page does not convert your result to that scale.

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
blocks.text: اقعد في مكان هادي من غير موبايل، وخلّي معاك حوالي ساعة وربع. الامتحان موديولين، كل واحد 27 سؤال في 32 دقيقة، يعني تقريبًا دقيقة وعشر ثواني للسؤال. جوه الموديول تقدر ترجع لأي سؤال، لكن لما الوقت يخلص الموديول بيقفل، وفي الامتحان الحقيقي مفيش رجوع لـ Module 1. مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط، فمتسيبش ولا سؤال فاضي. والنسبة اللي هتظهر في الآخر للتدريب بس، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 9
blocks.intro: Two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes each. In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest items, and Module 2 adapts to your Module 1 performance (it is harder or easier). In this practice test all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Once Module 1 ends, you cannot go back to it.

questions.p: Records kept by villagers living on the slopes of one volcano show that its activity has been ______: decades of near silence have been broken, without obvious warning, by short bursts of violent eruption.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: intermittent
continuous
predictable
declining
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: silence, then sudden bursts, then silence again, which is "intermittent." "Predictable" is ruled out by "without obvious warning."
ce: Correct: long quiet periods broken by short bursts describe activity that stops and starts, which is what "intermittent" means.
Opposite: "decades of near silence" means the activity was not continuous.
The eruptions came "without obvious warning," so they were not predictable.
The text describes a stop-start pattern, not activity that grows weaker over time.

questions.p: The first prototypes of the folding wheelchair designed by engineer Sherif Galal were so ______ that many users struggled to lift them into a car; later models, made of lightweight aluminum, weighed less than half as much.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: affordable
fragile
cumbersome
elegant
questions.e: Users struggled to lift the early chairs, and later models weighed less than half as much, so the early ones were heavy and awkward: "cumbersome." "Fragile" fails because the problem was weight, not strength.
ce: Price is not mentioned, and being cheap would not make a chair hard to lift.
Nothing says the chairs broke easily; the problem was lifting them.
Correct: chairs that are hard to lift and much heavier than later models are heavy and awkward, which is what "cumbersome" means.
Elegance has nothing to do with users struggling to lift the chairs.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
Mr. Hollins was not a man to be hurried. He read his morning newspaper ______, column by column and page by page, and if a visitor called before he had reached the end of the shipping news, the visitor waited in the hall.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: hastily
deliberately
reluctantly
secretly
questions.e: He will not be hurried and reads the paper column by column, so he reads slowly and carefully: "deliberately." "Reluctantly" fails because he clearly wants to finish the paper.
ce: Opposite: he is "not a man to be hurried."
Correct: reading slowly and in order, refusing to be hurried, is reading deliberately.
Nothing suggests he dislikes reading the paper; he insists on finishing it.
He reads openly, and visitors wait in the hall while he does.

questions.p: Documentary filmmaker Nour Hamdi rarely uses narration or interviews in her films. She prefers simply to ______ the daily lives of the fishing families she films, letting the camera record what they do without comment.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: observe
dramatize
criticize
interrupt
questions.e: Hamdi lets the camera record "without comment," so she watches rather than shapes or judges: "observe." "Dramatize" fails because it means adding drama, which she avoids.
ce: Correct: letting the camera record "without comment" means watching, which is what "observe" means.
Dramatizing means making events more exciting or theatrical, the opposite of recording without comment.
Criticizing would be a kind of comment, and she avoids comment.
Recording what the families do "without comment" is the opposite of interrupting them.

questions.p: City officials have often treated street vendors as obstacles that crowd sidewalks and slow down pedestrians. A study of three neighbourhoods by urban researcher Salma Ragab suggests another view. Streets where vendors worked into the evening had more people on them after dark, and residents said they felt safer walking there than on similar streets without vendors. Ragab argues that vendors, by keeping streets busy, benefit the whole neighbourhood.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To argue that street vendors should be removed from busy sidewalks
To present research suggesting that street vendors may benefit neighbourhoods in a way officials have overlooked
To describe how street vendors choose where to set up their stalls
To compare the incomes of vendors in three different neighbourhoods
questions.e: The text contrasts a common official view with a study showing an overlooked benefit (safer, busier streets). The "remove vendors" choice reverses the text's purpose.
ce: Reversed: this matches the officials' old view, which the text challenges.
Correct: the text sets the officials' view against Ragab's finding that vendors make streets busier and safer.
The text never discusses how vendors choose their locations.
Income is never mentioned.

questions.p: Acoustic engineers describe a concert hall by its reverberation time: how long a sound takes to fade away after it stops. A hall with a very short reverberation time makes an orchestra sound dry and thin, while one with a very long time blurs fast passages into a muddy wash of sound. Designers therefore aim for a time in between, and many modern halls include movable panels and curtains so that the reverberation can be adjusted for different kinds of music.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It describes a problem with orchestras and argues that musicians should play more slowly.
It tells the history of one concert hall and explains why it was rebuilt.
It presents a debate between engineers and then explains which side won.
It defines a term, describes the problems at two extremes, and explains how designers respond to them.
questions.e: The text first defines reverberation time, then shows what goes wrong when it is too short or too long, then explains the designers' solution. The "musicians should play more slowly" choice misreads a detail about fast passages.
ce: The problem is in the hall's design, and nothing suggests musicians should change their playing.
No single hall or rebuilding is mentioned.
There is no debate; the text explains one idea step by step.
Correct: definition of reverberation time → too short and too long → designers aim between and use adjustable panels.

questions.p:
Text 1
Many observers assume that people who move from villages to large cities gradually lose touch with the communities they left behind. In this view, city life, with its long working hours and new friendships, slowly replaces the ties of home.

Text 2
Sociologist Dina Fahmy surveyed 600 people living in a large city who had grown up in rural villages. Most visited their home villages several times a year, regularly sent money to relatives there, and belonged to city associations of people from the same village. These associations, Fahmy found, also help newcomers from the village find housing and work in the city.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Fahmy (Text 2) most likely respond to the assumption described in Text 1?
c: She would argue that migrants never form new friendships in the city.
She would agree that migrants lose touch with their villages but say it happens more quickly than observers think.
She would argue that the assumption overlooks the strong ties that many migrants keep with their home communities.
She would say that village associations make it harder for newcomers to settle in the city.
questions.e: The observers expect ties to fade; Fahmy found regular visits, money sent home and active associations, so she would say the assumption misses these strong ties. The "never form new friendships" choice goes far beyond what her study shows.
ce: Too extreme: Text 2 says nothing about migrants avoiding new friendships.
Reversed: her data show ties staying strong, not fading.
Correct: her survey shows visits, money sent home and village associations, which goes against the idea that ties fade.
Contradicted: the associations help newcomers find housing and work.

questions.p: As the oceans absorb carbon dioxide from the air, seawater becomes slightly more acidic. This change makes it harder for animals such as oysters, clams, and some kinds of plankton to build their shells, which are made of a mineral called calcium carbonate. Oyster hatcheries on the Pacific coast of the United States have already lost large numbers of young oysters when acidic water rose from the deep ocean toward the shore. Several hatcheries now test the seawater constantly and treat it before it enters their tanks.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Oyster shells are made of a mineral called calcium carbonate.
Ocean acidification makes it harder for some sea animals to build shells, a problem that has already affected oyster hatcheries.
Oyster hatcheries have solved the problem of ocean acidification.
The oceans absorb more carbon dioxide than the air does.
questions.e: The text explains how acidic water harms shell-building animals and gives hatcheries as an example, so the main idea joins both. The "solved the problem" choice overstates what treating tank water can do.
ce: Too narrow: a supporting detail, not the main idea.
Correct: it covers the general effect and the real-world example that the text develops.
Too extreme: hatcheries protect their own tanks, but the ocean is still becoming more acidic.
The text does not compare the amounts of carbon dioxide in the ocean and the air.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
Rosalind had been promised her grandmother's piano, and she had pictured it in her own small parlour a hundred times. But when the men came to move it, they found that it would pass through neither the door nor the window of her lodgings, and so it remained in her grandmother's empty house, where Rosalind went every Sunday afternoon to play it to the dust-sheets.
questions.q: According to the text, why does Rosalind play the piano at her grandmother's house?
c: She prefers the sound of the piano in her grandmother's house.
Her grandmother asked her to leave the piano where it was.
The piano could not fit through the door or the window of her lodgings.
Her lodgings are too noisy for her to practise there.
questions.e: The men could not fit the piano through her door or window, so it stayed in the grandmother's house, and Rosalind goes there to play. The other choices invent reasons the text never gives.
ce: Nothing compares the sound in the two places.
The text says the piano was promised to her, not that she was asked to leave it.
Correct: the text says the piano "would pass through neither the door nor the window," so it stayed in the old house.
Noise is never mentioned.

questions.p: Large rounded boulders lie scattered across a high hillside in one region, far above any river. Geologist Rasha Kamel hypothesizes that the boulders were carried there by an ancient glacier rather than by a river. Glaciers often scrape long, parallel scratches into the rock they slide over; rivers do not leave such marks.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kamel's hypothesis?
c: The bedrock beneath the boulders is covered with long, parallel scratches that all run in the same direction.
The boulders are rounded and smooth on all sides.
The hillside lies about 300 meters above the floor of the valley.
Rivers in the region flood every spring.
questions.e: The text gives a test: glaciers leave parallel scratches, rivers do not. Finding such scratches under the boulders supports Kamel. Rounded boulders are the tempting trap, but rounding fits both explanations.
ce: Correct: the text says glaciers leave such scratches and rivers do not, so this finding points to a glacier.
Both rivers and glaciers can round boulders, so this does not favour either idea.
The height of the hillside does not show how the boulders got there.
Present-day floods do not test whether an ancient glacier moved the boulders.

questions.p: In an original novel written in the style of the nineteenth century, the narrator suggests that the opening of a railway station changed the way the people of her town thought about time.
questions.q: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
c: "Some of the farmers complained that the noise of the engines frightened their cattle."
"The station was built of yellow brick, with a clock tower that could be seen from the river."
"The first train arrived on a wet Tuesday in March, and half the town turned out to see it."
"Before the trains came, the church bell had been our only clock, and no one minded if it rang a little late; now every man carried a watch and consulted it with an anxious face."
questions.e: The claim is about a change in thinking about time, so the quotation must show a before-and-after; only the church-bell quotation does. The clock-tower quotation mentions a clock but shows no change in attitude.
ce: It shows a complaint about noise, not about time.
It describes the building, not a change in how people thought about time.
It describes the first arrival but not a change in attitudes to time.
Correct: it contrasts a relaxed attitude to time before the railway with anxious watch-checking after it.

questions.p:
Households that own a car, by distance from the nearest metro station, in one city
Distance from nearest station | Households that own a car (%)
Less than 500 meters | 31
500 meters to 1 kilometer | 44
1 to 2 kilometers | 58
More than 2 kilometers | 71

A transport researcher studying one city noted that households living closer to metro stations were less likely to own a car.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's observation?
c: Only 31% of households living less than 500 meters from a metro station owned a car, compared with 71% of households living more than 2 kilometers away.
58% of households living 1 to 2 kilometers from a metro station owned a car.
Most households in the city owned a car.
Households living 500 meters to 1 kilometer from a station were more likely to own a car than households living 1 to 2 kilometers away.
questions.e: To support "closer means less likely to own a car," the answer must compare groups at different distances: 31% near the stations vs 71% far away. The single 58% figure is true but shows no comparison.
ce: Correct: it compares the closest and farthest groups and shows car ownership rising with distance.
True, but one figure alone cannot show a pattern linked to distance.
The table gives percentages for each distance group, not for the whole city, so this cannot be shown.
False: 44% is lower than 58%.

questions.p:
Students enrolled in music lessons at a community centre, by instrument
Instrument | 2020 | 2024
Oud | 24 | 41
Piano | 58 | 62
Violin | 30 | 27
Guitar | 45 | 52

The director of a community centre reported that although enrollment rose for most of the instruments taught there between 2020 and 2024, it did not rise for every instrument. For example, ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
c: enrollment in oud lessons rose from 24 students to 41.
enrollment in violin lessons fell from 30 students in 2020 to 27 in 2024.
piano had more students than any other instrument in both years.
enrollment in guitar lessons fell from 52 students to 45.
questions.e: The example must show an exception to the rise, and only violin fell (30 to 27). The guitar choice reverses the table's numbers.
ce: True, but it shows a rise, not an instrument that failed to rise.
Correct: the violin is the one instrument whose enrollment did not rise, so it is the needed example.
True, but it does not show an instrument whose enrollment failed to rise.
False: guitar rose from 45 in 2020 to 52 in 2024.

questions.p: Mud at the bottom of some lakes builds up in layers over thousands of years and traps pollen from the plants growing nearby. In the mud of one lake, layers from about 8,000 years ago are full of oak pollen, while layers from about 5,000 years ago contain mostly grass pollen and very little oak. Because oak trees need much more rainfall than grasses do, the researchers who studied the mud concluded that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the climate around the lake probably became wetter between about 8,000 and 5,000 years ago.
the climate around the lake probably became drier between about 8,000 and 5,000 years ago.
oak trees spread across the region about 5,000 years ago.
grass pollen is carried much farther by the wind than oak pollen is.
questions.e: Oak (needs much rain) gave way to grass (needs less), so the area most likely became drier. The "wetter" choice reverses the logic of the clue about rainfall.
ce: Reversed: a wetter climate would favour oaks, not grasses.
Correct: oaks need more rain, so a shift from oak to grass suggests less rainfall.
Contradicted: there is very little oak pollen in the 5,000-year-old layers.
Nothing in the text discusses how far pollen travels.

questions.p: The first telephone exchanges needed human operators, who connected every call by ______ automatic exchanges, which did not need operators, gradually replaced them during the twentieth century.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: hand
hand,
hand;
hand, and,
questions.e: "The first telephone exchanges needed… by hand" and "automatic exchanges… replaced them" are both complete, so a semicolon is needed. A comma alone creates a comma splice.
ce: Run-on: the two sentences are fused with no punctuation.
Comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.
Correct: both parts are complete sentences, and a semicolon joins two complete sentences.
The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

questions.p: In 1934, a travelling cinema brought films to one small village for the first time. When the lights went down and the projector began to ______ the audience fell completely silent.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: whir;
whir
whir,
whir:
questions.e: A dependent "When…" clause comes first, so a comma separates it from the main clause. A semicolon or colon would need a complete sentence before it.
ce: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side, and "When the lights went down…" is not one.
Without a comma, "whir the audience" reads as if the projector were whirring the audience, which is confusing.
Correct: a comma marks the end of the long introductory clause before the main clause "the audience… fell silent."
A colon must follow a complete sentence, and the "When…" clause is not complete.

questions.p: In her 1961 book The Death and Life of Great American ______ writer Jane Jacobs argued that busy sidewalks, short blocks, and a mix of old and new buildings make city neighbourhoods safer and livelier.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Cities, and
Cities;
Cities:
Cities,
questions.e: The sentence opens with a long prepositional phrase ("In her 1961 book…"), so a comma separates it from the main clause. A semicolon or colon would need a complete sentence before it.
ce: "And" would join a phrase to a full clause as if they were equal, which makes the sentence ungrammatical.
A semicolon needs a complete sentence before it, and the introductory phrase is not one.
A colon must follow a complete sentence, and the introductory phrase is not one.
Correct: a comma ends the long introductory phrase before the main clause "writer Jane Jacobs argued…"

questions.p: The thin, alternating light and dark layers of sediment that settle each year at the bottom of some glacial ______ allow scientists to count back through thousands of years, much as tree rings do.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: lakes;
lakes,
lakes
lakes—
questions.e: The long subject ends with "lakes," and "allow" is its verb, so no punctuation is needed. A comma is the trap: never put one between a subject and its verb.
ce: A semicolon needs a complete sentence before it, and the subject has no verb yet.
A single comma would separate the subject from its verb "allow."
Correct: "The thin… layers… of some glacial lakes" is the subject and "allow" is the verb; no punctuation goes between them.
A single dash would wrongly cut the subject off from its verb.

questions.p: In one coastal town, the outer walls of several of the oldest ______ are now decorated with murals painted by students from the local art school.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: buildings
building's
buildings'
buildings's
questions.e: "Several of the oldest ___" needs a plural noun, and the walls are already named earlier ("the outer walls of"), so no possessive is needed: "buildings." "Buildings'" is tempting, but it would need a noun after it.
ce: Correct: "several of the oldest buildings" needs a plain plural noun; nothing belongs to the buildings in this phrase.
Singular possessive: "several of the oldest" needs a plural, and no noun follows for it to possess.
Plural possessive, but no noun follows for the buildings to possess.
This form is never correct; a plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.

questions.p: Since the city installed sensors on its water pipes in 2019, engineers ______ hundreds of leaks before the leaks could cause serious damage. The sensors send an alert whenever the pressure in a pipe drops suddenly.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: have detected
detect
will detect
had detected
questions.e: "Since" + a past starting point that runs to now calls for the present perfect: "have detected." "Had detected" is the trap, but it would place everything before some other past event.
ce: Correct: "Since 2019" describes a period that began in the past and continues to now, which needs the present perfect.
Simple present does not fit an action counted from a starting point in the past.
Future tense contradicts the leaks already found since 2019.
Past perfect needs a later past moment to refer back from, and "since 2019" runs up to the present.

questions.p: Mangroves are among the few trees that can survive in seawater, and many coastal communities depend on them. Growing in salty, muddy water along tropical coasts, ______
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the shoreline is protected from storm waves by the thick, tangled roots of mangrove trees.
mangrove trees protect shorelines from storm waves with their thick, tangled roots.
storm waves are weakened by the thick, tangled roots of mangrove trees.
it is the thick, tangled roots of mangrove trees that protect shorelines from storm waves.
questions.e: The opening phrase describes what is growing along tropical coasts, so "mangrove trees" must follow it immediately. The "shoreline" choice is the closest trap: it sounds natural but says the shoreline is growing in the water.
ce: Dangling modifier: it says the shoreline is growing in salty water.
Correct: the mangrove trees are what grow in salty water, so they must come right after the opening phrase.
Dangling modifier: it says the storm waves are growing in the water.
Dangling modifier: the word right after the comma is the empty subject "it," which cannot be growing in water.

questions.p: Early pianos could play both soft and loud notes, depending on how hard the player struck the keys; that is why the instrument was first called the pianoforte, from the Italian words for "soft" and "loud." ______ the harpsichord, which came before the piano, played every note at roughly the same volume no matter how the keys were pressed.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Similarly,
By contrast,
As a result,
For example,
questions.e: The piano could vary its volume and the harpsichord could not, so the sentences contrast: "By contrast." "As a result" fails because the harpsichord came first and was not caused by the piano.
ce: The harpsichord is different from the piano, not similar.
Correct: the harpsichord's fixed volume is the opposite of the piano's soft and loud notes.
The piano's range of volume did not cause the earlier harpsichord's fixed volume.
The harpsichord is not an example of an instrument that plays soft and loud notes.

questions.p: Concrete is very strong when it is squeezed but weak when it is stretched, so a plain concrete beam can crack under its own weight if it is long enough. ______ builders often place steel bars inside concrete beams; the steel resists the stretching forces that the concrete alone cannot.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: For this reason,
However,
Meanwhile,
In contrast,
questions.e: Concrete's weakness under stretching is the reason builders add steel, so a cause-effect transition fits: "For this reason." "However" fails because nothing is being contrasted.
ce: Correct: steel is added because of the weakness described in the first sentence, a cause-and-effect link.
Adding steel does not go against the first sentence; it follows from it.
"Meanwhile" signals something happening at the same time, not a response to a problem.
The second sentence is a result of the first, not a contrast with it.

questions.p: During a survey of remote workers in one city, many respondents said that they now spent most weekdays in their own neighbourhoods, buying lunch at nearby shops and walking in local parks during breaks. ______ many of them had come to know their neighbours far better than they had when they commuted to an office every day.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: As a result,
Nevertheless,
For instance,
Previously,
questions.e: The first sentence describes more time spent locally, and the second gives the effect, so "As a result" fits. "For instance" fails because the second sentence is a consequence, not an example.
ce: Correct: spending weekdays in the neighbourhood led to knowing neighbours better, a cause and its effect.
Knowing neighbours better is not surprising after spending more time nearby, so a contrast is illogical.
Knowing neighbours is not an example of shopping and walking locally; it is a consequence of it.
The second sentence describes the present, after the change, not an earlier time.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Mohs scale is used to compare the hardness of minerals.
• It was created in 1812 by the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs.
• It ranks minerals from 1 (softest) to 10 (hardest).
• Talc is ranked 1, quartz 7, and diamond 10.
• A mineral can scratch any mineral with a lower number on the scale.
questions.q: The student wants to explain how the Mohs scale is used to compare minerals. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The Mohs scale was created in 1812 by the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs.
On the Mohs scale, minerals are ranked from 1 to 10 by hardness, and a mineral can scratch any mineral with a lower number, so quartz (7) can scratch talc (1).
Diamond, the hardest mineral on the Mohs scale, is ranked 10.
Friedrich Mohs created a scale to compare the hardness of minerals.
questions.e: To explain how the scale works, the sentence needs the 1-to-10 ranking and the scratch rule, ideally with an example; only one choice has them. The history choice is accurate but off-goal.
ce: History only; it does not explain how the scale works.
Correct: it explains how the ranking works and shows it with an example from the notes.
One fact about one mineral; it does not explain the scratch test.
It names the purpose but not how minerals are ranked or compared.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A film archive restored an Egyptian comedy made in the 1950s.
• The original film negative had been damaged by heat and humidity.
• The team scanned each frame of the film digitally.
• They repaired scratches and stains frame by frame.
• The restoration took 18 months.
• The restored film was shown at a festival in 2025.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize how difficult the restoration was. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The team scanned each frame of the 1950s comedy digitally before it was shown at a festival.
The restored 1950s comedy was shown at a festival in 2025.
A film archive restored an Egyptian comedy from the 1950s.
Because the original negative had been damaged by heat and humidity, the team had to repair scratches and stains frame by frame, work that took 18 months.
questions.e: Emphasizing difficulty means stressing the damage, the painstaking repairs and the 18 months; only one choice does that. The festival choice tells what happened afterwards instead.
ce: It mentions one step but does not stress the damage or the time needed.
It reports the result, not how hard the work was.
It names the project but says nothing about its difficulty.
Correct: it shows the damage, the slow frame-by-frame work and the long time it took, all stressing difficulty.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Sargasso Sea is a region of the North Atlantic Ocean.
• Unlike other seas, it has no land coastline.
• Instead, it is bounded on all sides by ocean currents.
• It is named after sargassum, a brown seaweed that floats on its surface.
• European and American eels travel there to lay their eggs.
questions.q: The student wants to explain what makes the Sargasso Sea unusual among the world's seas. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Unlike other seas, the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic has no land coastline; it is bounded on all sides by ocean currents instead.
The Sargasso Sea is named after sargassum, a brown seaweed that floats on its surface.
European and American eels travel to the Sargasso Sea to lay their eggs.
The Sargasso Sea is a region of the North Atlantic Ocean.
questions.e: The goal is to show what makes the Sargasso Sea unusual among seas, and the notes say it alone has no land coastline. The eel choice is a striking fact but does not compare it with other seas.
ce: Correct: it states what makes this sea unusual and contrasts it with other seas.
It explains the name, not what makes the sea unusual among seas.
An interesting fact, but it does not say how the sea differs from other seas.
It locates the sea but gives nothing unusual about it.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
Though her letters home were full of cheerful news, there was something ______ in them that troubled her brother: she wrote of picnics and dances and the colour of the sea, but never of herself, as though she had stepped aside from her own life in order to describe it from a distance.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: boastful
affectionate
careless
detached
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: she describes everything except herself, as if from a distance, so the letters feel "detached." "Affectionate" ignores the worrying distance that the text emphasizes.
ce: She never writes about herself, so she cannot be boasting.
Nothing about warmth troubles the brother; what worries him is her distance from her own life.
The letters are full of detail, so they are not careless.
Correct: writing about events "from a distance" and "never of herself" is emotionally distant, which is what "detached" means.

questions.p: The theory that the Moon formed from debris thrown into space when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth is not merely ______; it is supported by evidence such as the close chemical similarity between Moon rocks and rocks from Earth's mantle.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: unanimous
outdated
speculative
obscure
questions.e: "Not merely X; it is supported by evidence" means X must be the opposite of evidence-based: "speculative." "Outdated" fails because evidence and age are not opposites.
ce: A theory cannot be "unanimous"; only people's agreement can, and the sentence does not discuss agreement.
The sentence contrasts the blank with evidence, not with being modern.
Correct: "not merely speculative; it is supported by evidence" contrasts guesswork with evidence.
Being little-known is not the opposite of being supported by evidence.

questions.p: Although the engineers' report praised the overall design of the new bridge, its assessment of the support cables was notably ______: it noted signs of rust in several places and recommended further inspection before heavy trucks were allowed to cross.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: final
glowing
indifferent
cautious
questions.e: "Although" contrasts the praise with the cable assessment, and the report raised concerns and asked for more checks: "cautious." "Final" fails because the report explicitly calls for more inspection.
ce: Asking for further inspection means the judgment is not final.
Opposite: "Although" sets the cable assessment against the praise, so it was not glowing.
Recommending further inspection shows concern, not indifference.
Correct: noting possible problems and asking for more inspection before allowing trucks is a careful, cautious judgment.

questions.p: The harvest songs of one mountain village had been ______ orally for at least two centuries, passed from parents to children without ever being written down, until a team of researchers recorded them in 2019.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: rehearsed
invented
transmitted
forgotten
questions.e: The phrase "passed from parents to children" defines the blank: the songs were handed on, or "transmitted." "Rehearsed" describes practice, not passing songs across generations.
ce: Practising songs is not the same as passing them from one generation to the next.
The songs were already two centuries old; the text is about passing them on, not creating them.
Correct: "passed from parents to children" means handed on, which is what "transmitted" means.
Contradicted: the songs survived long enough to be recorded.

questions.p: Sociologist Heba Zaki's conclusions about how the new metro line has changed social life in the city are deliberately ______: she notes that her survey covered only three neighbourhoods and warns against applying its results to the city as a whole.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: sweeping
tentative
unfounded
celebrated
questions.e: She limits her claims because her survey was small, so her conclusions are "tentative." "Unfounded" is the trap: limited evidence is still evidence.
ce: Opposite: sweeping conclusions would apply to the whole city, which she warns against.
Correct: warning that the results may not apply city-wide shows that she holds her conclusions loosely, which is what "tentative" means.
Her conclusions are based on a survey, so they are not without foundation; they are only limited.
Nothing in the text says her conclusions are famous or praised.

questions.p: Satellite images show that many of the world's large river deltas are losing land along their coasts. Rising sea levels are part of the cause. But researchers point out that dams far upstream play a role as well. For thousands of years, rivers carried sand and mud to the sea and spread them across their deltas, constantly rebuilding the shoreline. Dams trap much of that material in their reservoirs, so less of it reaches the coast to replace what the waves wash away.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To explain how satellites measure changes in coastlines
To argue that all dams on large rivers should be removed
To point out a cause of coastal land loss in river deltas that is less obvious than rising sea levels
To show that rising sea levels play no part in the loss of delta land
questions.e: The main point comes after "But": dams far upstream also starve deltas of sediment, a less obvious cause. The "no part" choice contradicts the text, which accepts rising seas as one cause.
ce: Satellites are mentioned only as a source; how they measure is never explained.
Too extreme: the text explains an effect of dams but does not recommend removing them.
Correct: after naming rising seas, the text turns ("But") to explain how upstream dams also cause land loss.
Contradicted: the text says rising seas are "part of the cause."

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
The Marsdens' drawing room was the most fashionable in the county, and Mrs. Marsden saw to it that everyone knew so. There were cabinets of painted china, mirrors from Venice, and a clock that played a minuet on the hour. __Visitors generally admired all of it at length, and then, with some relief, asked whether they might sit in the garden.__
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It suggests, with gentle humour, that visitors find the room less pleasant than its owner believes.
It shows that visitors sincerely prefer the drawing room to any other room in the house.
It introduces the garden as the main setting for the rest of the story.
It explains why Mrs. Marsden chose to decorate the room with china and mirrors.
questions.e: Visitors dutifully admire the room and then escape "with some relief," a gently humorous hint that the showy room is not enjoyable. The "sincerely prefer" choice misses the irony of "relief."
ce: Correct: the visitors praise the room as expected but are relieved to escape it, which quietly mocks Mrs. Marsden's pride.
Reversed: their "relief" at leaving shows they do not prefer it.
Nothing suggests the story moves to the garden; the sentence comments on the room.
The sentence is about visitors' reactions, not her reasons for decorating.

questions.p:
Text 1
Earth's magnetic field has reversed its direction many times in the past, at irregular intervals, so that a compass that now points north would have pointed south. Some writers have warned that the next reversal could be a disaster for life on Earth, since the field helps shield the planet from harmful radiation from space.

Text 2
Geophysicist Mona Zaki agrees that the magnetic field weakens during a reversal, which can take thousands of years. But she notes that the fossil record shows no mass extinctions that match the timing of past reversals, even though many reversals have occurred during the long history of complex life.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Zaki (Text 2) most likely respond to the warnings described in Text 1?
c: She would claim that the magnetic field does not weaken during a reversal.
She would argue that Earth's magnetic field has never reversed.
She would agree that the next reversal will cause mass extinctions.
She would suggest that the warnings are not supported by the evidence from past reversals.
questions.e: Zaki accepts that the field weakens but points out that past reversals left no matching mass extinctions, so she would say the warnings lack support. The "never reversed" choice contradicts her own reference to past reversals.
ce: Contradicted: she "agrees that the magnetic field weakens."
Contradicted: she discusses past reversals as real events.
Reversed: her point is that past reversals did not.
Correct: if past reversals did not coincide with mass extinctions, the record does not support predictions of disaster.

questions.p: Explanations for why families leave city centres for the suburbs often focus on space: suburban homes tend to be larger and more likely to have gardens. But when sociologist Tamer Saad interviewed 300 families who had recently moved from the centre of one large city to its suburbs, most said that space mattered less to them than schools. Many reported that they would have stayed in the centre if they had found a school there that they trusted.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Saad's interviews suggest that, for many families, schools rather than space were the main reason for moving to the suburbs.
Suburban homes tend to be larger than homes in city centres.
Most families who move to the suburbs regret their decision.
Schools in city centres are generally better than schools in the suburbs.
questions.e: The text sets up the usual "space" explanation and then reports Saad's finding that schools mattered more; that finding is the main idea. The "larger homes" choice is just the background idea the text moves away from.
ce: Correct: this is the finding the text builds toward after "But."
A background detail from the common explanation, not the main idea.
Nothing in the text mentions regret.
Not supported: families said they could not find a school they trusted in the centre.

questions.p: Psychologist Laila Gamal hypothesizes that listeners find music most pleasing when it is moderately predictable. In her view, melodies that are too predictable bore listeners, while melodies that are too unpredictable confuse them.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Gamal's hypothesis?
c: In a study, listeners rated melodies of low, medium, and high predictability, and the medium-predictability melodies received the highest average ratings.
In a study, listeners gave the highest ratings to the least predictable melodies.
In a study, trained musicians gave higher ratings than other listeners to every melody.
In a study, listeners recognized familiar melodies faster than unfamiliar ones.
questions.e: Gamal predicts that the middle level of predictability is most pleasing, and the correct finding shows exactly that. The "least predictable rated highest" finding goes against her hypothesis.
ce: Correct: the middle level scoring highest is exactly what Gamal's "moderate is best" hypothesis predicts.
This would weaken the hypothesis, since the most unpredictable melodies would be best.
It compares groups of listeners, not levels of predictability.
Speed of recognition does not test which level of predictability is most pleasing.

questions.p: In an original novel written in the style of the nineteenth century, the narrator suggests that Mr. Fenwick's generosity comes more from a wish to be admired than from real concern for others.
questions.q: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
c: "His servants said that he had never once raised his voice to them."
"Every Christmas he sent a guinea to the fund for the county hospital."
"He was often seen walking alone by the river in the early morning."
"He gave handsomely to every subscription in the parish, provided that the list of donors was to be printed in the newspaper."
questions.e: The claim is about the motive behind his giving, and only the quotation with the condition "provided that the list of donors was to be printed" shows that he wants admiration. The hospital quotation shows giving but no motive.
ce: It shows good temper, not the reason for his generosity.
It shows generosity but says nothing about his motive.
It has nothing to do with generosity or admiration.
Correct: giving only when his name will be published shows that he gives in order to be seen and admired.

questions.p:
Sand eel numbers and puffin breeding success on one island
Year | Sand eel abundance index | Chicks raised per nest
2019 | 85 | 0.9
2020 | 40 | 0.3
2021 | 70 | 0.7
2022 | 30 | 0.2

Sand eels are the main food that puffins on one North Sea island bring to their chicks. A team of ecologists hypothesized that the puffins' breeding success depends heavily on the number of sand eels available.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the ecologists' hypothesis?
c: Puffins raised 0.7 chicks per nest in 2021.
The sand eel abundance index fell from 85 in 2019 to 30 in 2022.
Puffins raised the most chicks per nest in 2019, when the sand eel index was highest (85), and the fewest in 2022, when it was lowest (30).
The number of chicks raised per nest rose every year from 2019 to 2022.
questions.e: A hypothesis linking two variables needs data on both: the best and worst years for sand eels match the best and worst years for chicks. The "index fell" choice is true but covers only one variable.
ce: True, but one year alone cannot show a link between the two variables.
True, but it gives only sand eel numbers and says nothing about puffin chicks.
Correct: it links both variables, showing breeding success rising and falling with sand eel numbers.
False: it went 0.9, 0.3, 0.7, 0.2, falling overall.

questions.p:
Battery capacity remaining after repeated charging (% of original)
Battery type | 500 cycles | 1,000 cycles | 2,000 cycles
Type P | 95 | 91 | 84
Type Q | 92 | 80 | 61
Type R | 97 | 88 | 70

An engineer testing three types of rechargeable battery concluded that although Type R keeps more of its capacity than Type P at first, Type P is the more durable of the two over long use.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the engineer's conclusion?
c: All three types of battery kept less of their capacity after 2,000 cycles than after 500 cycles.
After 2,000 cycles, Type Q kept only 61% of its capacity, the least of the three types.
After 1,000 cycles, Type P kept 91% of its capacity.
After 500 cycles, Type R kept 97% of its capacity and Type P 95%, but after 2,000 cycles Type P kept 84% while Type R kept only 70%.
questions.e: The conclusion has two parts (R better at first, P better later), so the answer needs early and late figures for both P and R. The Type Q choice is accurate but about the wrong battery.
ce: True, but it does not compare P and R at all.
True, but the conclusion compares Types P and R, not Q.
True, but one figure for one battery cannot show either part of the comparison.
Correct: it shows both parts of the conclusion, R ahead early and P ahead after long use.

questions.p: Many of the world's deserts lie in two belts around 30 degrees north and 30 degrees south of the equator, where dry air sinks toward the ground. Other deserts form in a different way. When moist air blowing in from the ocean meets a mountain range, it is forced upward and cools, and most of its water falls as rain on the slopes facing the ocean. By the time the air crosses the mountains, it is dry. A geologist studying a mountain range near a coast where the wind usually blows in from the sea would therefore expect that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the far side of the mountains receives the most rain.
both sides of the mountains receive about the same amount of rain.
the slopes facing the sea receive more rain than the slopes on the far side of the mountains.
no desert can form near these mountains because they are close to the sea.
questions.e: Following the text's steps, moist sea air rains on the sea-facing slopes and arrives dry on the far side, so the sea-facing slopes are wetter. The "far side" choice reverses the process.
ce: Reversed: the air is already dry when it reaches the far side.
Contradicted: the air loses its water on one side and is dry on the other.
Correct: the moist air drops most of its rain on the sea-facing slopes, leaving the far side dry.
Contradicts the process described: this is exactly how such deserts form even near the coast.

questions.p: In a study of apartment buildings in one city, residents of buildings with a shared laundry room said they knew more of their neighbours than residents of buildings where each apartment had its own washing machine. The buildings were similar in size, age, and rent. The researchers also found that residents of the shared-laundry buildings who usually did their washing late at night, when the room was nearly empty, knew no more neighbours than residents of the other buildings. These findings suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: residents of buildings with private washing machines prefer not to know their neighbours.
meeting other people while using the shared room, rather than simply living in a building that has one, helps residents get to know their neighbours.
the amount of rent residents pay determines how many neighbours they know.
residents who do their washing late at night know more neighbours than those who wash during the day.
questions.e: Night-time users had the shared room but met no one, and they knew no more neighbours; so meeting people, not just having the room, makes the difference. The "wash late at night" choice reverses the night-time finding.
ce: Nothing in the text describes what those residents prefer.
Correct: only those who used the room when others were there knew more neighbours, so the encounters are what matter.
The buildings had similar rents, so rent cannot explain the difference.
Reversed: the night-time users knew no more neighbours than residents of the other buildings.

questions.p: The oldest surviving complete piece of music with written notation, the Seikilos ______ was carved on a marble column in what is now Turkey about two thousand years ago.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: epitaph;
epitaph
epitaph,
epitaph—
questions.e: "The Seikilos epitaph" renames the subject and is set off by a pair of commas, so a comma must follow "epitaph." A dash fails because the pair must match.
ce: A semicolon would cut the subject off from its verb "was carved."
The extra information opened with a comma, so it must close with one before the verb "was carved."
Correct: the comma closes the extra information "the Seikilos epitaph," which opened with the comma after "notation."
A dash cannot close extra information that was opened with a comma.

questions.p: The engineers building the new metro line faced a difficult ______ the tunnel had to pass beneath a river without disturbing the foundations of the historic bridge above it.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: problem, being that
problem,
problem
problem:
questions.e: The first part is complete and the second explains what the problem was, so a colon is right. A comma alone would create a comma splice.
ce: "Being that" is not a standard way to join clauses, and the comma does not fix the sentence.
Comma splice: "the tunnel had to pass…" is a complete sentence and cannot be joined with a comma alone.
Run-on: two complete sentences run together with no punctuation.
Correct: a complete sentence comes first, and what follows explains the problem, so a colon fits.

questions.p: Phytoplankton—tiny drifting organisms that, like plants, use sunlight to make their own ______ produce roughly half of the oxygen released on Earth each year. Most of them are far too small to be seen without a microscope.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: food
food,
food—
food;
questions.e: "Tiny drifting organisms… food" is extra information opened by a dash, so it must close with a dash. The comma is tempting because of the commas around "like plants," but that pair is already closed.
ce: Without a closing dash, the description runs straight into the verb, and the sentence loses track of its subject.
A comma cannot close information that opened with a dash; and the comma pair "that, like plants," is already complete.
Correct: the extra information opened with a dash, so it must close with a dash before the verb "produce."
A semicolon would cut the subject "Phytoplankton" off from its verb "produce."

questions.p: The film's score contains no conventional instruments at all. Instead, composer Amal Rashed built it entirely from recordings of everyday ______ the creak of a wooden door, the hiss of a kettle, and the rumble of a passing tram.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: sounds;
sounds:
sounds, including:
sounds
questions.e: A complete sentence ends at "sounds," and a list follows, so a colon is correct. The semicolon fails because a list is not a complete sentence.
ce: A semicolon must join two complete sentences, and the list is not a complete sentence.
Correct: the sentence before the blank is complete, and a colon introduces the list of sounds.
A colon should not come after "including"; it must follow a complete sentence.
With no punctuation, the list runs straight into "sounds" and the sentence is confusing.

questions.p: The collection of letters, diaries, and photographs that residents donated to the town's new local history museum ______ now on display in the museum's main hall.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: have been
are
were
is
questions.e: Strip away "of letters… museum" and the subject is "The collection," which is singular: "is." "Are" is the trap, because a list of plural nouns sits right before the blank.
ce: Plural verb; the singular subject "collection" needs "has," not "have."
Plural verb: it agrees with "letters, diaries, and photographs" or "residents," which are not the subject.
Plural and past, while "now" calls for the present.
Correct: the subject is "The collection" (singular), so it takes "is."

questions.p: By the time Charles Dickens began publishing Great Expectations in 1860, he ______ one of the most famous novelists in the English-speaking world for more than twenty years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: had been
has been
is
will have been
questions.e: "By the time" + a past event and "for more than twenty years" call for the past perfect: "had been." "Has been" is the trap, but it links to the present, not to 1860.
ce: Correct: the past perfect shows a state that lasted up to an earlier past moment ("By the time… in 1860").
The present perfect connects to the present, but this is all before 1860.
The present tense does not fit a nineteenth-century situation.
The future perfect looks forward from now, not back to 1860.

questions.p: The company's new electric scooter looks almost the same as its older model. The battery in the new scooter, however, charges fully in two hours, far faster than ______ which needs nearly six hours to charge.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the older model,
that of the older model,
those of the older model,
the older models,
questions.e: Like must be compared with like: the new battery with the old battery, which "that of the older model" expresses. "The older model" is the classic trap: it compares a battery to a scooter.
ce: Faulty comparison: it compares the battery with a whole scooter.
Correct: "that of the older model" means "the battery of the older model," so a battery is compared with a battery.
"Those" is plural, but it must stand for the singular "battery."
Faulty comparison: it compares one battery with several whole scooters, and "which needs" no longer matches.

questions.p: Scientists still cannot predict the day or hour when an earthquake will strike. ______ they can estimate the chance that a strong earthquake will occur in a given region within the next few decades, and such estimates guide the building rules that cities set for new construction.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: For example,
As a result,
Even so,
Likewise,
questions.e: The first sentence states a limit, and the second gives something scientists can still do, so the transition must concede and contrast: "Even so." "As a result" wrongly makes the limit the cause of the ability.
ce: Long-term estimates are not an example of failing to predict exact times.
Being unable to predict exact times does not cause scientists to be able to estimate long-term chances.
Correct: despite not being able to predict exact times, scientists can still make useful long-term estimates, a concession and contrast.
Making useful estimates is not similar to being unable to predict; it contrasts with it.

questions.p: Many nineteenth-century novels first appeared in magazines in monthly parts, and authors often ended each part at a moment of suspense so that readers would buy the next issue. ______ even when these novels were later printed as complete books, many of their chapters still ended with cliffhangers.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Previously,
Nevertheless,
Meanwhile,
Consequently,
questions.e: Serial publication caused authors to end parts in suspense, so the printed chapters still show that effect: "Consequently." "Nevertheless" fails because nothing unexpected follows.
ce: The second sentence describes what happened later, not earlier.
Cliffhangers in the books are not surprising after the first sentence; they are expected.
"Meanwhile" signals events at the same time, but the books came later, as a result of the serial form.
Correct: the chapters ended in suspense because they were first written as monthly parts, a cause and its effect.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Urban researcher Omar Halim studied how people use public plazas in one city.
• Plaza 1 has movable chairs; at lunchtime it averaged 210 visitors per hour.
• Plaza 2 is similar in size and location but has only fixed benches; it averaged 90 visitors per hour at lunchtime.
• Halim suggests that movable chairs let people choose sun or shade and arrange themselves in groups.
questions.q: The student wants to present the study's main finding along with Halim's explanation for it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Urban researcher Omar Halim studied two public plazas of similar size and location in one city.
Halim suggests that movable chairs let people choose sun or shade and arrange themselves in groups.
Plaza 1 averaged 210 visitors per hour at lunchtime, while Plaza 2 averaged 90.

Halim found that a plaza with movable chairs drew 210 visitors an hour at lunchtime, more than twice as many as a similar plaza with fixed benches, perhaps because movable chairs let people choose sun or shade and sit in groups.
questions.e: The goal has two parts, the finding and its possible explanation, and only one choice contains both. The figures-only choice is the strongest trap: it gives the numbers but no explanation and does not even mention the chairs.
ce: It introduces the study but gives neither the finding nor the explanation.
It gives the explanation but not the finding it explains.
It gives the finding but not the explanation, and it does not say what makes the plazas different.
Correct: it gives the finding (210 vs 90) and Halim's explanation for it.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Ring of Fire is a zone that follows the edges of the Pacific Ocean.
• It contains most of the world's active volcanoes.
• Along much of the Ring of Fire, plates of Earth's crust meet.
• In many of these places, one plate slides beneath another and sinks into the mantle.
• The sinking plate helps produce magma, which rises to form volcanoes.
questions.q: The student wants to explain why the Ring of Fire has so many volcanoes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The Ring of Fire, which follows the edges of the Pacific Ocean, contains most of the world's active volcanoes.
The Ring of Fire has so many volcanoes because, along much of it, one plate of Earth's crust slides beneath another, and the sinking plate helps produce magma that rises to the surface.
Along much of the Ring of Fire, plates of Earth's crust meet.
Most of the world's active volcanoes are found in a zone around the Pacific Ocean.
questions.e: Explaining why requires the cause-and-effect chain: plates meet, one sinks, magma forms and rises. The "contains most of the world's active volcanoes" choice describes the zone but gives no reason.
ce: It states that there are many volcanoes but not why.
Correct: it gives the cause (one plate sinking beneath another) and the result (magma that forms volcanoes).
It gives one part of the cause but does not connect it to volcanoes.
It restates where the volcanoes are without explaining their cause.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Composer Nadia Amin writes new scores for silent films from the 1920s.
• The films are screened with a live orchestra.
• In the 1920s, silent films were often accompanied by musicians playing in the theatre.
• Amin studies surviving 1920s cue sheets, lists of music suggested for each scene of a film.
• She writes for instruments that were common in cinemas of the time, such as piano and violin.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize Amin's efforts to make her scores historically accurate. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: To keep her scores true to the period, Amin studies surviving 1920s cue sheets and writes for instruments that were common in cinemas of the time, such as piano and violin.
Amin writes new scores for silent films from the 1920s, which are screened with a live orchestra.
In the 1920s, silent films were often accompanied by musicians playing in the theatre.
Cue sheets are lists of music suggested for each scene of a film.
questions.e: Her effort to be accurate is shown by two actions, studying cue sheets and choosing period instruments, and only one choice combines them. The live-orchestra choice describes her work in general, not the accuracy.
ce: Correct: it gives both of her methods for historical accuracy and states that aim directly.
It describes her work but not her effort to be historically accurate.
Background history only; Amin is not mentioned.
It defines a term but does not show what Amin does with cue sheets.

blocks.title: After the test
items: **Read every explanation**, including those for questions you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason, not by luck. Each choice has its own short reason.

**List your weak skills.** Use your score by skill and write down every skill where you lost two or more questions, plus the trap that caught you (reversed, too extreme, half-right, off-topic, nearest-noun, comma splice…). The "Study these again" links take you straight to the lessons.

**Go back to the matching lessons:** Words in Context and High-Value Vocabulary for SAT Reading and Writing; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences; Sentence Boundaries; Extra Information: Commas, Dashes and Brackets in Pairs; Semicolons; Colons; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement; Verb Tense and Aspect; Verb Finiteness; Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers; Plurals and Possessives; Transitions; Rhetorical Synthesis (Student Notes).

**Redo every question you missed** after the lesson and its practice page, without looking at the explanation, and say aloud why each wrong choice is wrong. Then take Practice Test 10 under the same timed conditions.
**Check your timing.** If you did not finish a module, study Time Strategy and How to Attack Every Question before your next full test.
